newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: Now South Africa awaits all-important S&P upgrade.
newsitem.headline: Now South Africa awaits all-important S&P upgrade.

text.p: South Africa looks well-placed to win a coveted investment grade rating from Standard and Poor's Corp later this year after being assigned BBB minus by Duff & Phelps Credit Rating Co on Wednesday.
The bullish rating from the second-tier U.S. agency had limited significance in itself, but was a sign of improving sentiment towards South Africa following recent economic reforms, economists said.

"It's a good indication. The importance really is that it suggests there might be an upgrade from the more important credit rating agencies," said Nico Czypionka, chief economist at Standard Bank in Johannesburg.

South Africa's long-term foreign currency debt currently straddles investment grade. Moody's Investors Service Inc rates the country an investment grade prospect at Baa3. But S&P has it pegged one notch below at BB plus, though with a positive outlook.

S&P is expected to visit South Africa around September or October and Guido Cipriani, S&P director responsible for South Africa, said in May that prospects had improved since the agency's last visit in September 1996.

Mike Brown, chief economist at SocGen Frankel Pollak, is confident of an upgrade following a cut in the 1997/98 budget deficit, a recent sharp rise in foreign reserves and important exchange control relaxation effective from July 1.
"I'd be surprised if they don't upgrade us," Brown said.

"I think we've met the monetary and fiscal targets, we've got the reserves and we are dismantling exchange controls. We are basically there -- our only element of risk is crime and violence, and I'm not sure how they will mark us on that."
A consistent investment grade view from the world's two top rating agencies, Moody's and S&P, would cut South Africa's borrowing costs by making its debt more attractive to global investors.

South African Finance Minister Trevor Manuel, speaking in Tokyo, said the bullish rating from Duff & Phelps meant Pretoria would be able to access a wider array of capital sources in the U.S. where many funds are barred from buying speculative paper.
The Duff & Phelps rating was commissioned ahead of the government's forthcoming Yankee bond issue, expected to total around $500 million with a maturity of 20 years.

Duff & Phelps said its rating view reflected the strong commitment of the government to establish a competitive and creditworthy economy, backed up by its medium-term Growth, Employment and Redistribution (Gear) strategy.
However, the rating was constrained by continued high fiscal deficits, low domestic savings, high unemployment, still relatively low reserves and high crime rates.

IBCA, the only other agency to have rated South Africa in the last two years, currently has the country on a speculative BB. A company official said on Wednesday that IBCA was unlikely to review this rating until November or December.
